newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair urges Welsh to back devolution plan.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair urges Welsh to back devolution plan.

text.p: British Prime Minister Tony Blair travelled to the former mining town of Nelson in Wales on Friday to plead his case for a Welsh assembly.

Blair spelled out the arguments in favour of devolution in front of 200 people from across Wales invited to take part in the prime minister's second "people's question time" since his Labour party swept to power on May 1.

Whereas plans for a Scottish parliament are expected to be approved handsomely in a referendum on September 11, polls show the plebiscite a week later on whether to set up a Welsh assembly will be a much closer-run thing.

A similar proposal by the previous Labour government was roundly rejected in 1979 by a four-to-one margin and powerful voices are being raised against it again now -- including some in Labour's parliamentary ranks.

But Blair, who earlier told reporters that Labour members would be "perfectly entitled" to speak their own mind in the run-up to the referendum, said the global trend toward decentralising power meant the time was now ripe for Wales to have a measure of home rule.
"If you look around and see how the rest of the world is developing, we have in Britain one of the most centralised governments anywhere in the western world," he said.

A directly elected Welsh assembly would give people democratic control over sevn billion pounds ($11 billion) of public spending, which is now overseen by officials in the Welsh Office answering to Welsh Secretary Ron Davies.

"If I was here in Wales, I'd be voting for it because I think it gives you the best chance of a more accountable government. I think we've spent far too long in this country over the past few years building up government by quango," Blair said.

Labour is committed to scaling back the number of quangoes -- an acronym for Quasi-Autonomous Non-Governmental Oranisations -- whose members are appointed directly by ministers and thus escape direct parliamentary oversight.

Judging by Friday's "Talk to Tony" session, held at a living history museum devoted to the Civil War of the 1640s, the state of cash-strapped schools and hospitals is a more burning issue in Wales than whether to create an assembly.
But one woman, Pat Chown, took Blair to task for refusing to give the assembly the same tax-raising powers that the Scottish parliament will enjoy.
"As a Welsh person, it makes me feel that we're not trusted," Chown, the chief executive of a housing association, told Reuters later.
Blair argued that Scotland was a different case, in part because it has its own legal and education systems.
"It's always possible to say yes, we should have gone further, but I think this is a very important step," he said.
